newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Issing- German prices in wrong direction.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Issing- German prices in wrong direction.

text.p: Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said on Friday that German price developments were moving in the wrong direction.
The Boersen-Zeitung newspaper cited Issing as saying that German price developments were moving "in the wrong direction" in all areas.
The newspaper did not indicate when the interview took place. A copy of the interview was released in advance of planned publication on Saturday.
Issing also said the Bundesbank's inflation goal of 1.5 to two percent, which forms the basis for its money supply growth target, had become more ambitious.
"The price estimate was ambitious and has now clearly become more ambitious," he said.

The newspaper, without providing direct quotes, also cited Issing as saying current Bundesbank monetary policy, with a securities repurchase rate at 3.00 percent, was less expansive than it was in August 1996.

In a separate interview on Tuesday, Issing said the central bank was worried by the mark's rapid slide against the dollar and dismissed the idea that Germany's economy was too weak to bear an interest rate rise.
The Boersen-Zeitung said Issing said the present currency situation had altered significantly the environment for monetary policy.

Issing also made clear that neither the imminent start of monetary union nor the general situation in Germany would limit the Bundesbank's ability to take action, should it feel it necessary to make a monetary policy move, the Boersen-Zeitung said.
It was necessary to keep an eye on further developments in M3 money supply, the Bundesbank's key policy indicator, Issing was indirectly quoted as saying.
Issing also said that the future European Central Bank would be operating in an "extremely difficult" phase since unemployment would still be at a critical level.
It would be bad to overburden the ECB with excessive potential for inflation, the paper quoted Issing as saying.
"The ECB would have to suffer the consequences of the things that we do wrong in terms of stability policies," Issing said.
However Issing said the Bundesbank would carry out its monetary policy according to the national situation, not the broader European context, the newspaper said.
"The deutschemark is an anchor currency, we are not determining an EU inflation index," he said.
